The problem with this is a problem with capitalism in general. There is far more money to be made no competing than there is in competing once a 'winner' in a given industry or region has emerged. The other company doesn't remain just blissfully unaware of what's happening. Let's say you spend billions of dollars getting infrastructure, marketing, and all this other important stuff set up. You get a few customers who'd go to you just to spite being screwed for so long, but people are generally lazy and if there's no price difference they're not going to move over. A long winded article that pushes 'the shared public good' while barely hinting at franchise monopolies.

This story and comments on here dance around the idea of a natural monopoly. Cable providers are natural monopolies. They have a high fixed/start up cost. But very low marginal cost. In a competetive market they would be forced to charge a price that would make it extremely difficult to cover their fixed costs. Thus a monopoly emerges out of necessity.

Nope. They're monopolies by government decree. In most areas of the US it is illegal to start a competing cable service. Where there is competition it is usually because of quirks in the law, e.g. Verizon FIOS utilized their telephony monopoly.

Proof: Railroads were even higher fixed/startup costs. Numerous were the cases were they would build parallel routes. Often to poke the finger in the other guys eye. Again,this action was only ended through legislative fiat.

The key point behind a natural monopoly is not the high fixed costs. It's the extremely low marginal cost. This is because in a competitive market, the price firms will set will end up being equal to their marginal cost. So although rail ways may or may not be natural monopolies. The fact that railways sometimes built next to each other in the past wouldn't change that. The theory behind this describes how the economy works in the long run. That doesn't mean a firm won't be stupid and try to build another rail line, just that if rail ways really are a natural monopoly, than it won't stay that way.

As far as the legislation goes. I would argue that although there are protection laws in a lot of places, a natural monopoly would exists regardless of the protection. As is reflected in the market in places without laws limiting competition, the monopolies still exist.

So somebody might argue, "well, if a natural monopoly would exist anyways, why should cable companies spend the money to lobby for these laws?". Although I don't know the answer to this I could make a few hypothesis. One it might be in place to protect less competitive cable companies from being forced out of there business by more competitive companies.

Maybe this sounds like I'm contradicting myself. But I really am not. Although I'm saying a firm could outcompete other firms to win a market. A natural monopoly is a phenomenon in which in the long run only one firm would still operate. So a more competetive firm could enter a market that will support a natural monopoly and force the other firm to leave the market. But long run competition would not exist.
